specStatements.text: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem.
A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.

The future of the human species on Earth relies on us maintaining a good level of biodiversity. Many human activities are reducing biodiversity and only recently have measures been taken to try to stop this reduction.

Rapid growth in the human population and an increase in the standard of living mean that increasingly more resources are used and more waste is produced. Unless waste and chemical materials are properly handled, more pollution will be caused.
Pollution can occur: in water, from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals; in air, from smoke and acidic gases; on land, from landfill and from toxic chemicals.
Pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.
Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.

The destruction of peat bogs, and other areas of peat to produce garden compost, reduces the area of this habitat and thus the variety of different plant, animal and microorganism species that live there (biodiversity).
The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas has occurred to: provide land for cattle and rice fields; grow crops for biofuels
Students should be able to describe some of the biological consequences of global warming.
Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, and contribute to 'global warming'.
Students should be able to describe both positive and negative human interactions in an ecosystem and explain their impact on biodiversity.
Scientists and concerned citizens have put in place programmes to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity.

These include: breeding programmes for endangered species; protection and regeneration of rare habitats; reintroduction of field margins and hedgerows in agricultural areas where farmers grow only one type of crop; reduction of deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions by some governments; recycling resources rather than dumping waste in landfill.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification gives only two reasons for large-scale tropical deforestation - to provide land for cattle and rice fields, and to grow crops for biofuels. No other causes of deforestation, and no named countries, species or data, are introduced.

The specification requires only that levels of carbon dioxide and methane are increasing and contribute to global warming, plus a description of some biological consequences. The chemistry of the greenhouse effect, the sources of each gas and any quantitative treatment of temperature change are not covered.
Only the five programmes listed in the specification are used as examples of positive human interaction; no additional conservation schemes, legislation or named organisations are introduced.

misconceptions.question: A pond contains 500 frogs of one species. A second pond contains 50 organisms belonging to 12 species. Which pond has the greater biodiversity?
misconceptions.correct: The second pond, because it contains the greater variety of different species.
misconceptions.misconception: Biodiversity means how many individual organisms there are, so the pond with the most organisms has the highest biodiversity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet population size and biodiversity in the same topic, and 'more living things' feels like 'more biodiversity'. Counting individuals is also the easier thing to do in a practical survey.
misconceptions.correction: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem. It is judged by the variety of species present, not by the number of individuals.

misconceptions.question: A nature reserve contains woodland, grassland and a lake. Does this by itself tell you the reserve has a high biodiversity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Biodiversity depends on the variety of different species present, not on how many habitats the reserve contains.
misconceptions.misconception: Biodiversity means the number of different habitats or ecosystems in an area.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Habitats are the visible, easily counted feature of a site, and textbooks often illustrate biodiversity with pictures of contrasting habitats, so students transfer the word from species to places.
misconceptions.correction: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem. A variety of habitats may support many species, but it is the variety of species that is measured.

misconceptions.question: Why does a great biodiversity make an ecosystem more stable?
misconceptions.correct: Because it reduces the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.
misconceptions.misconception: The more species there are, the more each species depends on the others, so a high biodiversity makes an ecosystem less stable and losing species makes it more stable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that organisms in a food web are interdependent, and assume that more species must mean more links and therefore more risk, rather than more alternatives.
misconceptions.correction: A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment. Losing species reduces stability.

misconceptions.question: Sewage and fertiliser drain into a river. Is this pollution?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Pollution can occur in water from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals.
misconceptions.misconception: Sewage and fertiliser are natural materials, so they cannot be pollution; only manufactured toxic chemicals count as pollutants.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'pollution' is popularly linked with chemical spills and factory smoke, and 'natural' is often treated as meaning harmless.
misconceptions.correction: Pollution can occur in water, from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals; in air, from smoke and acidic gases; and on land, from landfill and from toxic chemicals. Pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.

misconceptions.question: A farm is extended and a quarry is opened on nearby grassland. Does this reduce the land available for other animals and plants?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.
misconceptions.misconception: Only building takes land away from wildlife; farmland and quarries are open countryside, so they leave the land available for other animals and plants.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Farmland looks green and 'natural' compared with towns, so students do not picture it as land removed from other species, even though a crop field supports few species.
misconceptions.correction: Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste. All four activities take habitat away from other species.

misconceptions.question: Peat is dug out of a peat bog and sold as garden compost. How does carbon dioxide get into the atmosphere?
misconceptions.correct: The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is only released if the peat is burned, so peat used as garden compost does not add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Combustion is the release process students meet most often, and decay is slow and invisible, so it is not recognised as a source of carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.correction: The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Peat spread on soil as compost decays, so carbon dioxide is still released.

misconceptions.question: Tropical forest is cleared to grow crops for biofuels. What happens to biodiversity in that area?
misconceptions.correct: Biodiversity falls, because the forest habitat and the species living in it are destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: Because biofuels are a renewable fuel, growing crops for biofuels cannot damage an ecosystem or reduce biodiversity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Biofuels are presented as an environmentally friendly alternative to fossil fuels, so students assume every consequence of producing them must also be beneficial.
misconceptions.correction: Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas has occurred to provide land for cattle and rice fields and to grow crops for biofuels. Clearing the forest destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity, whatever the crop is used for.

misconceptions.question: Which gases named in the specification are increasing in the atmosphere and contribute to global warming?
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the only gas that contributes to global warming; methane is a separate problem that does not affect it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carbon dioxide dominates news coverage and earlier topics on combustion and photosynthesis, so methane is remembered only as a product of decay or digestion.
misconceptions.correction: Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing, and both contribute to 'global warming'.

misconceptions.question: Give a biological consequence of global warming.
misconceptions.correct: Loss of habitat, changes in the distribution of species, or changes in migration patterns.
misconceptions.misconception: The only biological consequence of global warming is that organisms get too hot and die where they are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Warming is understood as a temperature problem, so students think about heat directly killing organisms rather than about habitats being lost or species moving to areas that now suit them.
misconceptions.correction: Biological consequences of global warming include loss of habitat, changes in the distribution of species and changes in migration patterns, as well as effects on individual organisms.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the biodiversity of an ecosystem?

options.text: The total number of individual organisms there
options.rationale: A student who believes biodiversity is a count of individuals picks the option about numbers of organisms. Biodiversity is the variety of different species, so a large population of one species is a low biodiversity.

options.text: Number of different habitats found in the area
options.rationale: A student who believes biodiversity means the range of habitats chooses this. The specification defines biodiversity by the variety of species, not by the number of habitats.

options.text: The number of species that depend on one another
options.rationale: A student who believes biodiversity is about how strongly species are linked selects this. Dependence between species relates to stability; biodiversity itself is simply the variety of species present.

options.text: The variety of the different species living there
options.rationale: Biodiversity is the variety of all the different species of organisms on earth, or within an ecosystem.

mcqs.stem: A woodland has a great biodiversity. Why is this ecosystem more stable?

options.text: The number of individual organisms stays the same
options.rationale: A student who equates biodiversity with numbers of individuals reads stability as unchanging population size. Stability comes from reduced dependence of one species on another, not from fixed numbers.

options.text: Each species depends more on others for shelter
options.rationale: A student who believes more species means more dependence chooses this. A great biodiversity reduces, rather than increases, the dependence of one species on another.

options.text: One species depends less on others for its food
options.rationale: A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems by reducing the dependence of one species on another for food, shelter and the maintenance of the physical environment.

options.text: The area contains a larger number of habitats
options.rationale: A student who defines biodiversity by habitats explains stability that way. The specification links stability to reduced dependence between species, not to a count of habitats.

mcqs.stem: As the human population grows, more untreated sewage and fertiliser drain into a river and many fish and plants die. What is the effect on the river?

options.text: There is no pollution as both are natural materials
options.rationale: A student who believes only manufactured chemicals pollute picks this. Pollution can occur in water from sewage, fertiliser or toxic chemicals.

options.text: Pollution kills organisms and biodiversity falls
options.rationale: More waste is produced as the population grows, and unless it is properly handled more pollution is caused; pollution kills plants and animals which can reduce biodiversity.

options.text: Biodiversity is unchanged as fish numbers recover
options.rationale: A student who treats biodiversity as a count of individuals thinks it is restored when numbers rise. Biodiversity falls when species are lost, whatever happens to the numbers of survivors.

options.text: Biodiversity falls but the ecosystem becomes stable
options.rationale: A student who believes fewer interdependent species means more stability chooses this. A great biodiversity ensures stability, so losing species makes the ecosystem less stable.

mcqs.stem: Part of an area of grassland is quarried for stone and the rest is ploughed to grow crops. What is the effect on other animals and plants?

options.text: Less land is available for other plants and animals
options.rationale: Humans reduce the amount of land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste, which reduces biodiversity.

options.text: Quarrying reduces the land but farming does not
options.rationale: A student who sees farmland as still being countryside picks this. Humans reduce the land available for other animals and plants by building, quarrying, farming and dumping waste.

options.text: Biodiversity is unchanged as many individuals stay
options.rationale: A student who equates biodiversity with numbers of individuals sees no change. Biodiversity is the variety of species, which falls when habitat is lost.

options.text: The ecosystem is more stable once species are lost
options.rationale: A student who believes species depend on each other too much for stability chooses this. A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems, so losing species reduces stability.

mcqs.stem: A peat bog is drained and the peat is dug out and sold as garden compost. What are the effects?

options.text: The habitat is lost and carbon dioxide is released
options.rationale: The destruction of peat bogs to produce garden compost reduces the area of this habitat, and thus its biodiversity, and the decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

options.text: Carbon dioxide is released by burning, not by decay
options.rationale: A student who links carbon dioxide release only to combustion picks this. The decay or burning of the peat releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

options.text: Biodiversity is unchanged as many organisms survive
options.rationale: A student who counts individuals rather than species sees no loss. Destroying the bog reduces the variety of plant, animal and microorganism species living there.

options.text: The land stays available because it is not built on
options.rationale: A student who thinks only building removes habitat chooses this. Digging out peat destroys the habitat itself, so the land is no longer available to the species that lived there.

mcqs.stem: A large area of tropical forest is cleared to grow crops for biofuels. What is the impact on biodiversity?

options.text: Biodiversity is unchanged because biofuels are renewable
options.rationale: A student who assumes a renewable fuel has no harmful effects picks this. Large-scale deforestation destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity whatever the land is then used for.

options.text: Biodiversity falls when the cleared trees are burned
options.rationale: A student who links harm only to burning chooses this. The loss of biodiversity is caused by clearing the forest habitat, not only by what happens to the felled trees.

options.text: Biodiversity falls as the forest habitat is destroyed
options.rationale: Large-scale deforestation in tropical areas, including clearance to grow crops for biofuels, removes the habitat and so reduces the variety of species living there.

options.text: Biodiversity falls, so the ecosystem becomes more stable
options.rationale: A student who believes fewer species means less dependence picks this. A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems, so losing species reduces stability.

mcqs.stem: Levels of carbon dioxide and methane in the atmosphere are increasing. Which is a biological consequence of the global warming this causes?

options.text: Species die out where the air becomes much warmer
options.rationale: A student who thinks warming only kills organisms directly picks this. Species may instead lose habitat, change their distribution or change their migration patterns.

options.text: Some species change the areas where they are found
options.rationale: Biological consequences of global warming include loss of habitat, changes in the distribution of species and changes in migration patterns.

options.text: Areas near carbon dioxide sources are affected most
options.rationale: A student who treats carbon dioxide as the single, local cause chooses this. Carbon dioxide and methane are both increasing in the atmosphere and contribute to global warming worldwide.

options.text: Ecosystems become more stable as species are lost
options.rationale: A student who believes species are made vulnerable by depending on each other picks this. A great biodiversity ensures the stability of ecosystems, so losing species reduces stability.

mcqs.stem: A government wants to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity. Which policy would have a positive impact?

options.text: Growing more crops that will be used to make biofuels
options.rationale: A student who believes biofuels are always beneficial picks this. Growing biofuel crops has driven large-scale tropical deforestation, which reduces biodiversity.

options.text: Spreading extra fertiliser on farmland each season
options.rationale: A student who does not count fertiliser as a pollutant sees this as harmless help for plants. Fertiliser draining into water is a cause of pollution, which kills plants and animals.

options.text: Digging up more peat bogs to sell as garden compost
options.rationale: A student who thinks unburned peat is harmless chooses this. Destroying peat bogs reduces the area of the habitat and its biodiversity, and the decaying peat releases carbon dioxide.

options.text: Reducing deforestation and carbon dioxide emissions
options.rationale: Reduction of deforestation and of carbon dioxide emissions by some governments is one of the programmes put in place to reduce the negative effects of humans on ecosystems and biodiversity.
